subject: deep-learning
question: Will an 8,000-word contract fit within the 8,000-token window?

artifact.setup:
Model context window: 8,000 tokens.
Plan: fit an 8,000-word English contract plus instructions into one prompt.

ai_claim: Yes. A context window of 8,000 tokens holds 8,000 words, so the contract fits exactly.

ai_solution.text: The window is 8,000 tokens.
A token is a word.
The contract has 8,000 words.
So it fits.

failure.explanation: Tokenisers split text into sub-word pieces. English averages roughly 1.3 tokens per word (about 0.75 words per token), so 8,000 words is about 10,500 tokens - well over the window, before adding instructions and leaving room for the answer. Count tokens with the model's tokenizer.
failure.why_convincing: For short common words, a token often is a word.

canonical_solution: No: 8,000 words is roughly 10,500 tokens. Count with the tokenizer and chunk or summarise.

valid_evidence.summary: 8,000 words x 1.3 tokens per word = 10,400 tokens > 8,000
The tokenizer reports 10,650 tokens for the contract.

counterexamples: Legal words like 'indemnification' split into several tokens.

hints.text: Check how text is split into tokens.
Step 2 equates tokens with words.
English averages about 1.3 tokens per word.
Estimate the token count of 8,000 words.
Step 2 is wrong: 8,000 words is about 10,500 tokens.

repair: Count tokens with the model's tokenizer; split the contract or use a larger-context model.
debrief: Budgets for context, cost and rate limits are in tokens. Measure them with the actual tokenizer.

subject: deep-learning
subtopic: Test questions in the fine-tuning data
question: Is 97% a trustworthy estimate of the fine-tuned model's accuracy on new support questions?

artifact.process:
A support dataset of 20,000 Q&A pairs was scraped from the help centre. 1,000 pairs were set aside as the test set; fine-tuning used all 20,000 pairs, including those 1,000.
Result: test accuracy 97%.

ai_claim: Yes. The test set is a separate list of 1,000 questions, and the model answered 97% correctly.

ai_solution.text: 1,000 pairs were set aside as a test set.
The model was fine-tuned on the dataset.
It answered 97% of the test questions correctly.
So its accuracy on new questions is about 97%.

failure.explanation: The 1,000 test pairs were also in the fine-tuning data, so the model has seen the exact questions and answers. 97% measures memorisation. Remove the test set (and near-duplicates) from the training data, and evaluate on questions the model has never seen.
failure.why_convincing: The test set was 'set aside' as a list, even though it was not held out from training.

canonical_solution: No: the test pairs were part of the training data. Exclude them (and near-duplicates) and re-evaluate.

valid_evidence.summary: Fine-tuning used all 20,000 pairs, including the 1,000 test pairs.
On 500 newly written questions, accuracy is 78%.

counterexamples: Rephrased versions of the test questions score far lower.

hints.text: Check which data the model was trained on.
Step 2 does not exclude the test set.
Test data must never appear in training data.
Evaluate on newly written questions.
Step 2 is wrong: the test pairs were trained on. The 97% is memorisation.

repair: Hold out the test set before fine-tuning and deduplicate near-copies.
debrief: Contamination is the main threat to LLM evaluation. Check for exact and near-duplicate overlap between training and test data.

subject: deep-learning
question: Is quarterly fine-tuning a sound way to make the assistant answer with current prices and stock?

artifact.plan: Fine-tune an LLM every quarter on the product catalogue so it can answer questions about current prices and stock.
artifact.context: Prices change daily; about 5% of products change stock status each hour.

ai_claim: Yes. Fine-tuning on the catalogue teaches the model the products and their prices, so it can answer accurately.

ai_solution.text: The catalogue contains products, prices and stock.
Fine-tuning teaches the model this information.
The model then knows current prices and stock.
So it can answer accurately.

failure.misconception: Using fine-tuning to store changing facts
failure.explanation: Fine-tuning bakes information into weights as of the training date. Prices change daily and stock hourly, so within days the model confidently gives stale answers - and fine-tuning is unreliable at making models recall specific facts precisely anyway. Retrieve current data at question time (RAG or tool calls to the catalogue API); use fine-tuning for style and task format.
failure.why_convincing: Fine-tuning does change what a model 'knows', which makes it seem like the way to add knowledge.

canonical_solution: No: facts that change daily go stale in weights. Retrieve current prices and stock at query time.

valid_evidence.summary: About 5% of products change stock status every hour; prices change daily.
A price changed yesterday is answered with last quarter's value.

counterexamples: The day after fine-tuning, some answers are already wrong.

hints.text: Compare how often the data change with how often the model is updated.
Step 3 assumes the model stays current.
Fine-tuning suits behaviour and format; retrieval suits changing facts.
Consider a price that changed yesterday.
Step 3 is wrong: fine-tuned facts go stale. Retrieve live data.

repair: Answer from live data via retrieval or tool calls; fine-tune only for tone and task format.
debrief: Put facts that change where they can be updated instantly: in a database the model queries, not in its weights.

subject: deep-learning
question: How many trainable parameters does LoRA add for this matrix?

artifact.code:
# LoRA with rank r = 8 on one 4096 x 4096 weight matrix W
# W is frozen; the update is B @ A with A: (r x 4096) and B: (4096 x r)
# AI working: trainable parameters = 4096 x 8 = 32,768

ai_claim: 32768. The low-rank update has 4096 x 8 = 32,768 parameters.

ai_solution.text: LoRA freezes W.
It trains a rank-8 update.
The update has 4096 x 8 parameters.
So 32,768 are trainable.

failure.misconception: Counting only one of the two low-rank matrices
failure.explanation: The update B A uses two matrices: A has 8 x 4096 = 32,768 parameters and B has 4096 x 8 = 32,768. Total 65,536 - still only 0.39% of the 16,777,216 in W.
failure.why_convincing: Each factor is one '4096 x 8' shape, so counting one feels complete.

canonical_solution: A and B together: 2 x 4096 x 8 = 65,536 trainable parameters.
counterexamples: A and B each hold 32,768 parameters.

hints.text: List the trainable tensors.
Step 3 counts one matrix.
LoRA's update is a product of two low-rank matrices.
Add the sizes of A and B.
Step 3 is wrong: both A and B are trained. Total 65,536.

debrief: LoRA's efficiency comes from 2 x d x r versus d x d. Counting both factors gives the true, still tiny, budget.

subject: deep-learning
question: Is the AI right that this trains the model to predict each next token from only the tokens before it?

artifact.code:
# tokens: (batch, T) integer ids
logits = model(tokens[:, :-1])                  # predictions for positions 1..T-1
loss = F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, V), tokens[:, 1:].reshape(-1))
# model uses causal self-attention

ai_claim: Yes. The inputs are tokens 0..T-2 and the targets are tokens 1..T-1, so each position is trained to predict the following token, and the causal mask keeps it from seeing later tokens. Cross-entropy over the vocabulary is the standard loss.

ai_solution.text: Inputs are the sequence without its last token.
Targets are the sequence shifted left by one.
Position t's prediction is compared with token t + 1.
Causal attention restricts position t to tokens 0..t, so there is no leakage.

canonical_solution: Correct. Shift-by-one targets with causal attention and cross-entropy is the standard autoregressive training setup.

valid_evidence.summary: tokens [A, B, C, D]: inputs [A, B, C], targets [B, C, D]

hints.text: Line up inputs and targets.
Step 4 depends on the causal mask.
Autoregressive LMs predict token t + 1 from tokens up to t.
Write out inputs and targets for a 4-token sequence.
This solution is correct. The shift and mask implement next-token prediction. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: The whole pretraining objective of a GPT-style model fits in three lines. Most bugs are in the shift or the mask.
